summary: An experimental document that describes IPP from a high level, provides a roadmap to the suite of IPP specifications, and gives background and rationale for the working group's major decisions.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains how the Internet Printing Protocol divides printing into a model, a message format, and a way to transfer messages. That separation lets the printing rules stay independent of the format and transport.

questions: what is the internet printing protocol
what is the ipp job id
subtitle: Why IPP separates the meaning of a print job from its encoding and transport.

tldr.problem: Internet printing needs a shared way for clients to request printer information, submit jobs, and manage those jobs.
tldr.mechanism: IPP separates a printer-and-job model from the binary encoding and the HTTP transfer used to carry requests and replies.
tldr.outcome: This Experimental RFC explains the IPP/1.0 design and its document set. Its IESG note expected a later standards-track version to change parts of the protocol.

today: RFC 2568 is an Experimental RFC and is not marked as obsoleted or updated in this unit's metadata. Its IESG note says a future standards-track version was expected to include changes, including stronger authentication and privacy features.

sections.title: The IPP Document Set
sections.content:
Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) lets a client ask about a printer, submit a print job, and ask about or cancel jobs. RFC 2568 is the overview and rationale document in a set that also includes design goals, a model, an encoding and transport specification, an implementer's guide, and a mapping to the Line Printer Daemon protocol.

IPP version 1.0 focuses on end-user functions. Operator and administrator requirements are outside its scope. The separate documents explain different parts of the same protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: IPP lets a program ask a printer about its features, send work, and manage print jobs. This RFC is the guide to the other documents that define those rules.

sections.title: The Printer and Its Three Layers
sections.content:
IPP describes exchanges between a client and a server called the Printer. The Printer can be a physical output device or a service that connects to output devices. The client sends information such as a job name and print settings; the Printer accepts or rejects the job and returns a response.

The design has three parts. The Model defines printing data and its meaning. The Encoding turns that data into a transferable form. The Protocol carries requests and responses between client and Printer. A directory schema also describes Printer attributes that a client can search.
sections.plainLanguage: IPP separates the meaning of a print request, its message format, and its delivery. A client sends the request to a Printer, which replies whether it accepted the job.

sections.title: Why the Model Stands Apart
sections.content:
The Model is independent of the encoding and transport. A product can keep printing information in its own data structures and convert it when sending or receiving messages. If another encoding or transfer method is needed later, the Model need not change.

A print job has both a Job URI and a Job ID. The URI allows a job to move between printers without changing its identifier. The numeric Job ID supports systems that can identify jobs only with a 32-bit positive integer; it is unique only within the Printer that received the create request.
sections.plainLanguage: The printing rules do not depend on one message format or delivery method. Each job has a URI and a number so clients with different capabilities can identify it.

sections.title: A Compact Binary Encoding
sections.content:
The encoding represents Model data as a sequence of attributes. Each attribute has a name and a value. A name has a length and uses a restricted set of ASCII characters. Values can be single items or sequences, and each value includes a length and a tag describing its type.

A complete request or response includes a version, an operation or status, parameters, and encoded attributes. A request may also carry print data after the Model data. The simple structure was chosen to make embedded printers easier to develop.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message contains named values, with information about each value's length and type. A printer can read these fields to understand the request.

sections.title: HTTP as the Transfer Method
sections.content:
IPP transfers its encoded requests and responses using HTTP 1.1 POST. RFC 2568 proposes no changes to HTTP. The authors chose an existing transfer method because it was widely deployed and already handled features such as persistent connections, chunked data, redirects, URLs, and extensible headers.

HTTP also suited network printers that could provide web-based help and status pages. POST was selected for sending print data. The RFC says other mechanisms could meet many of the same goals, so the listed reasons do not uniquely dictate the choice.

For security, the design uses HTTP digest authentication for access control and SSL3 for secure communication. The RFC notes that SSL3 is not on the IETF standards track and that stronger security features were expected in a later version.
sections.plainLanguage: IPP sends its messages with HTTP POST, so it does not need a new transfer protocol. The RFC's security choices were HTTP digest authentication and SSL3.
